claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
The proposed improvements are primarily governed by a refined, chemically heterogeneous microstructure.
The refined, chemically heterogeneous microstructure promotes grain-boundary sliding.
Heterogeneous interfaces activate additional plastic-deformation mechanisms, including dislocation nucleation.
The relevant WTaTiVZr microstructure contains heterogeneous elemental segregation at grain boundaries.
The relevant WTaTiVZr microstructure contains nanoscale Zr-rich or Ti-rich precipitates.
The proposed nanoscale precipitates serve as dislocation-nucleation sites.
Chemical complexity in WTaTiVZr produces localized lattice-parameter variations and residual stress fields.
The proposed residual stress fields promote grain-boundary sliding.
The proposed residual stress fields mitigate crack propagation.
The heterogeneous microstructure provides alternative plastic-deformation pathways that enhance toughness relative to more homogeneous pure tungsten.
At 800–1200 °C under equivalent loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater plastic strain at failure than pure tungsten.
At 800–1200 °C under equivalent loading, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater resistance to crack initiation and propagation than pure tungsten.
Regions with finer, chemically varied grain boundaries and localized precipitates will correlate with enhanced deformation.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply between 800 and 1200 °C.
Temperatures outside 800–1200 °C, oxidation, or environments inducing additional phases may change the dominant deformation mechanisms.
